paragraphs: ASGO starts from the observation that neural-network parameters have meaningful matrix and tensor structure. Treating them simply as a collection of individual numbers can miss useful patterns. The paper focuses on two commonly observed patterns: gradients often have low rank, and the Hessian, which describes local curvature, is approximately block diagonal.

The proposed optimizer uses these structures through an adaptive preconditioner. A preconditioner changes how a gradient translates into a parameter update; here, its updates depend on structured gradients. The purpose is to make optimization respond to relationships within the parameters, rather than leaving those relationships unused.

The authors prove improved convergence rates relative to existing structured-gradient methods in their theoretical analysis. They also use that theory to show how low-rank gradients and block-diagonal curvature can benefit ASGO. Practical modifications are evaluated on language-model tasks, providing empirical support for the algorithm. The contribution therefore connects an optimization design to both mathematical convergence results and observed training effectiveness.
neurips-2025-asgo-adaptive-structured-gr.tldr: ASGO adapts gradient updates to neural-network structure, with improved theoretical convergence rates and empirical support on language-model tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models connect visual and language inputs directly to robotic decisions. BadVLA investigates whether these models can contain a persistent backdoor: a behavior that remains hidden during ordinary tasks but changes control when a particular trigger appears. The paper identifies this as a concern for systems whose training may be provided as a service.

Its approach separates the attack into two objectives. First, it makes trigger-related representations distinct from representations of benign inputs. Second, it introduces control deviations conditioned on that trigger while retaining performance on clean tasks. Separating these objectives is central to making the unwanted behavior selective and difficult to notice through ordinary task accuracy alone.

Across multiple VLA benchmarks, the authors report attack success rates close to 100% with little effect on clean-task accuracy. Further evaluations find that the attack withstands common input perturbations, task transfers, and model fine-tuning. These findings expose a security weakness in the evaluated models: strong ordinary performance can coexist with persistent, trigger-dependent failures in robotic control.
neurips-2025-badvla-towards-backdoor-att.tldr: BadVLA demonstrates persistent, trigger-dependent control failures in vision-language-action models while largely preserving ordinary task performance.

paragraphs: A model can sometimes fit every training example, including noisy ones, yet still perform close to optimally on new data. This phenomenon is called benign overfitting. The paper studies when it occurs in a single-head softmax attention model, extending an analysis previously developed for linear models and fully connected or convolutional networks.

For a classification setting, the authors prove that benign overfitting can appear after just two gradient-descent steps under appropriate conditions. They also establish conditions for benign overfitting in a minimum-norm or maximum-margin interpolator. These results examine both a short training process and a solution characterized by its norm or margin.

The key quantity is the signal-to-noise ratio, defined here through the relative norms of signal and noise tokens. Within the studied setting, a sufficiently large ratio is both necessary and sufficient for benign overfitting. This gives the result a precise boundary: fitting noisy data successfully depends on the strength of the useful signal relative to noise, rather than following automatically from the use of attention.
neurips-2025-benign-overfitting-in-singl.tldr: The paper characterizes when single-head attention can fit noisy training data yet generalize well, identifying signal-to-noise ratio as decisive in its setting.

paragraphs: Nonlinear activations are usually valued because they let networks represent more complicated functions. This paper identifies an additional benefit of ReLU in wide networks: it changes the geometry relevant to gradient-based training. The authors compare networks with their nonlinear activations enabled against corresponding networks with those activations disabled.

With ReLU, similar inputs become more separated in the feature space defined by model gradients. The neural tangent kernel, which captures relationships among these gradient features, also has a smaller condition number. Increasing depth strengthens both effects. In the specific limit where width becomes infinite before depth, all data have the same fixed angular separation in that feature space.

The linear comparison behaves differently: adding depth preserves the original input separation, and its kernel conditioning remains equivalent to that of the input Gram matrix. Because kernel conditioning is closely connected to convergence theory, the findings imply improved worst-case convergence rates for gradient-based methods. The result concerns training geometry in the analyzed wide-network setting, alongside the familiar expressive benefits of nonlinearity.
neurips-2025-better-ntk-conditioning-a-f.tldr: In wide networks, ReLU improves gradient-feature separation and neural tangent kernel conditioning, implying better worst-case optimization rates.

paragraphs: Models used to discover molecules must predict properties for candidates that may differ substantially from their training data. BOOM evaluates this out-of-distribution challenge through a chemically informed benchmark of common molecular-property tasks. Its focus is whether models remain useful when prediction moves beyond familiar examples, a central requirement for discovering novel molecules.

The study evaluates more than 150 model-task combinations. No evaluated model generalizes strongly across every task, and even the best-performing model has an average out-of-distribution error three times its in-distribution error. The authors also find that current chemical foundation models do not demonstrate strong extrapolation. Models with strong built-in assumptions can nevertheless perform well on tasks involving simple, specific properties.

Extensive ablations examine how data generation, pretraining, hyperparameter optimization, architecture, and molecular representation affect these outcomes. This makes BOOM useful for investigating where generalization succeeds or breaks down, beyond simply ranking models. The findings emphasize the gap between performance on familiar molecular data and reliable prediction for novel chemical candidates.
neurips-2025-boom-benchmarking-out-of-di.tldr: BOOM reveals substantial weaknesses in molecular-property prediction beyond training distributions across more than 150 model-task combinations.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations by comparing samples from altered versions of a graph. CaliGCL addresses two ways these comparisons can become misleading. Different components of a representation can cancel one another's evidence of similarity, while random graph alterations can change a sample's meaning enough to invalidate its assigned positive or negative relationship.

The method tackles similarity estimation by splitting representation vectors into smaller partitions. It measures similarity within these pieces and applies exponential scaling to emphasize aligned components while reducing the influence of conflicting ones. A separate discriminator checks whether augmented pairs remain semantically consistent and enables corrections to misleading training signals.

These components address different parts of the learning process: how similarity is measured and whether the pair itself provides appropriate supervision. Together, they guide the encoder toward representations that better preserve meaning despite graph augmentation. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report reduced effects from both biases and state-of-the-art performance, supporting the value of calibrating both the comparison measure and the sample assignments.
neurips-2025-caligcl-calibrated-graph-co.tldr: CaliGCL improves graph contrastive learning by refining similarity measurements and correcting sample pairs whose meaning changes during augmentation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to detect interactions whose text suggests the possibility of significant harm. The aim is to recognize when an interaction may warrant closer monitoring. Rather than requiring a separate language model to analyze every case, the authors investigate probes that read internal activations already produced by the model being monitored.

Several probe architectures are trained using synthetic data and evaluated on diverse real-world data outside that training distribution. The probes show robust generalization in these evaluations. Their performance is comparable to prompted or fine-tuned medium-sized language-model monitors, while their reported computational requirements are lower by six orders of magnitude.

The efficiency comes from reusing existing activations, which makes the monitoring step much cheaper than another substantial model evaluation. The experiments also suggest a possible hierarchical system: probes could provide an inexpensive initial filter and flag cases for more costly downstream analysis. The paper supports that direction as a resource-aware monitoring strategy, while its demonstrated contribution is efficient detection of potentially high-stakes interactions.
neurips-2025-detecting-high-stakes-inter.tldr: Activation probes detect potentially high-stakes interactions with performance comparable to larger monitors at dramatically lower computational cost.

paragraphs: Sampling a discrete distribution is difficult when only unnormalized scores are available. Markov chain Monte Carlo provides a principled approach, but its transitions can explore the possibilities slowly. Discrete Neural Flow Samplers instead learn a sampling process, aiming to make movement through the discrete space more efficient.

DNFS learns the rate matrix of a continuous-time Markov chain, which controls transitions between states. Training seeks dynamics that satisfy the Kolmogorov equation describing how probabilities evolve. The objective involves an intractable partition function, so the authors use control variates to reduce noise in its Monte Carlo estimation. This leads to a coordinate-descent learning algorithm.

A locally equivariant transformer provides the rate-matrix parameterization. The authors report that this design improves training efficiency while retaining expressive modeling capacity. Empirical evaluations cover sampling unnormalized distributions, training discrete energy-based models, and solving combinatorial optimization problems. Together, these applications demonstrate the usefulness of learning discrete sampling dynamics, with both the estimation procedure and network design contributing to computational efficiency.
neurips-2025-discrete-neural-flow-sample.tldr: DNFS learns continuous-time transitions for efficient discrete sampling, combining variance-reduced training with a locally equivariant transformer.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge between neural networks often involves reusing entire parameter sets, even when only some of that knowledge is useful. Selecting smaller portions can require handcrafted rules or rigid assumptions about network structure. ECO proposes learning reusable components through an evolutionary process, with the aim of retaining essential, transferable knowledge more efficiently.

The framework represents these components, called learngenes, as neural circuits. Its Genetic Transfer Learning procedure generates diverse populations of networks, selects high-performing members, and passes their learngenes to later generations. Repeating this process is intended to let common knowledge accumulate within modular circuits through supervised learning and selection.

The resulting components support initialization and transfer across models and tasks. Extensive experiments report strong generalization and efficient initialization, together with substantial reductions in computation and memory relative to conventional approaches. The evolutionary analogy therefore guides a concrete transfer mechanism: reusable circuits are refined through repeated selection, making the unit of transferred knowledge smaller and more modular than a complete network parameter set.
neurips-2025-eco-evolving-core-knowledge.tldr: ECO evolves reusable neural circuits that transfer knowledge across models and tasks while reducing computational and memory costs in experiments.

paragraphs: Complex robotic manipulation requires procedural knowledge about how a task breaks into steps and executable actions. The paper argues that inaccurate procedural knowledge limits existing language-model planners beyond simple pick-and-place tasks. It also addresses the computational burden of relying on very large language models for embodied systems.

The proposed hierarchical procedural knowledge graph links household tasks to their steps and then to atomic actions a robot can understand. This structure connects human-level instructions with the action detail needed for manipulation. An automatic construction framework powered by multiple language-model agents builds the graph, which contains more than 40,000 activity steps across over 6,000 household tasks.

Experiments show that adding this knowledge graph significantly improves planning with 7B-parameter models, allowing them to outperform standalone 72B-parameter models in the evaluations. The approach also improves GPT-4o. These results support structured procedural knowledge as a way to strengthen robotic planning while reducing the model scale required, rather than relying entirely on knowledge stored inside a larger planner.
neurips-2025-enhancing-llm-planning-for-.tldr: A hierarchical procedural knowledge graph improves robotic planning, with graph-assisted 7B models outperforming standalone 72B models in experiments.

paragraphs: ENMA addresses prediction of physical systems described by time-dependent, parameterized partial differential equations. These systems can vary across physical parameters and dynamical regimes, while observations may be incomplete or uncertain. The paper introduces a generative neural operator to predict future spatial and temporal behavior under those conditions.

Its representation pipeline first uses attention to map irregularly sampled spatial observations into uniform latent representations. A spatial and temporal convolutional encoder compresses them further. A masked autoregressive transformer then predicts future dynamics token by token in this compressed space, using a flow-matching training loss. This connects irregular observations to a compact generative representation of evolving physical fields.

At inference time, ENMA can condition on earlier states from the target trajectory or on auxiliary trajectories with similar dynamics. That conditioning enables in-context adaptation using the supplied examples. The authors report generalization to new PDE regimes and support for one-shot surrogate modeling. The central contribution is a generative operator that combines flexible observation encoding with example-conditioned prediction of future dynamics.
neurips-2025-enma-tokenwise-autoregressi.tldr: ENMA generates future PDE dynamics token by token in a compressed space, adapting through context from past states or related trajectories.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a hand interacting with an object requires separating persistent shape from appearance changes caused by lighting and movement. Existing approaches using implicit representations can depend on dense three-dimensional annotations or short clips with restricted motion and scene conditions. HOGS targets more general hand-object modeling from unconstrained monocular RGB imagery.

The framework uses three-dimensional Gaussian splatting and combines image-based photometric cues with the physically grounded structure of the Gaussian representation. Its central aim is to disentangle inherent geometry from temporary changes in appearance. This distinction matters because an asset whose geometry is entangled with one lighting condition or motion pattern may not transfer well to another.

The authors report that HOGS enables hand-object assets to generalize to unseen environments and dynamic movement patterns. Experiments on two challenging datasets show better monocular reconstruction and photorealistic rendering than state-of-the-art methods. These results support its representation strategy as a way to improve both visual reconstruction and the reuse of reconstructed assets across changing conditions.
neurips-2025-generalizable-hand-object-m.tldr: HOGS uses 3D Gaussians to separate hand-object geometry from changing appearance, improving reconstruction and generalization in evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Diffusion solvers for combinatorial optimization can spend extra inference compute on more denoising steps, but the resulting gains often saturate quickly. GenSCO explores a different use of that computation: repeated search cycles in which generation helps move between candidate solutions. Each cycle combines local-search disruption with diffusion sampling.

This design encourages exploration beyond the current solution's neighborhood instead of repeatedly refining the same candidate. Training supports the search loop through a rectified-flow model that learns trajectories from suboptimal solutions toward optimal ones. A lightweight transformer models the associated neural differential equations and helps linearize those trajectories, accelerating the improvement obtained from additional search.

Experiments report large gains over previous neural optimization methods and substantial speedups against the classical solver LKH3 at specified solution-quality targets. GenSCO reaches a reported 0.000% optimality gap on TSP-100 with a 141-fold speedup, and a 0.02% gap on TSP-500 with approximately a tenfold speedup. These comparisons show how search-driven generation can make extra inference computation more productive in the evaluated problems.
neurips-2025-generation-as-search-operat.tldr: GenSCO turns diffusion generation into a repeated search operation, improving inference-time scaling and achieving substantial reported routing-solver speedups.

paragraphs: FunDPS reconstructs full solutions of partial differential equations from extremely sparse or noisy measurements. It treats the unknown as a function and samples possible solutions conditioned on observations. This allows the method to represent a posterior distribution over solutions, which matters when limited measurements leave uncertainty about the complete physical field.

The method first trains an unconditional denoising model using neural operators, with a design that is independent of a particular discretization. During inference, gradient-based guidance adjusts generated samples to satisfy the available observations. The authors extend Tweedie's formula to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, providing a mathematical foundation for this function-space posterior sampling approach.

Across five PDE tasks with only 3% observation, FunDPS reports an average accuracy improvement of 32% over state-of-the-art fixed-resolution diffusion baselines while using four times fewer sampling steps. Multi-resolution fine-tuning further supports transfer across resolutions and faster sampling. The results connect sparse-data reconstruction with resolution flexibility, addressing both the information shortage and the fixed-grid dependence of the compared approaches.
neurips-2025-guided-diffusion-sampling-o.tldr: FunDPS combines function-space diffusion with observation guidance to reconstruct PDE solutions from sparse data across resolutions.

paragraphs: This paper studies algorithms that use previously encountered problem instances to propose solutions for future ones. Its online-learning framework evaluates performance over a sequence, rather than treating each instance independently. For each instance, performance is the ratio between the algorithm's solution cost and that instance's optimal cost; these ratios are then averaged.

The authors apply this framework to k-median clustering and give an efficient learning algorithm. Its theoretical guarantee is to approximately match the average performance of the best single fixed k-median solution chosen after seeing the entire sequence. That hindsight comparator is an important part of the result: it provides a common solution against which the evolving algorithm is assessed.

Experiments show performance close to optimal and automatic adaptation when the sequence changes dynamically. This empirical adaptability complements the guarantee against a fixed hindsight solution. The contribution is both a way to formalize learning from repeated optimization instances and an efficient clustering algorithm that uses experience to improve decisions across a changing sequence.
neurips-2025-learning-augmented-algorith.tldr: An online learning framework yields an efficient k-median algorithm with a fixed-hindsight comparison guarantee and empirical adaptation to changing instances.

paragraphs: LLM-PySC2 makes StarCraft II accessible as an environment for evaluating language-model decision-making. It addresses two interface problems: access to the hundreds of actions available through pysc2 and native support for collaboration among multiple agents. The environment supplies the complete action space together with multimodal information and game Wiki knowledge.

An asynchronous query architecture supports interaction with language models while maintaining constant latency as the agent population scales. The experiments examine both broad strategic decisions and detailed operations. They include established StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge tasks as well as newly proposed scenarios, giving the evaluation multiple levels of decision-making complexity.

The tested models can win complex scenarios, but they do not consistently choose correct actions, especially with the full action space and multiple agents. Without task-relevant instructions, pretrained models show hallucinations and inefficient collaboration. These findings make the environment useful for exposing weaknesses that remain despite occasional successful play, while providing infrastructure for further work on language-model planning and coordination.
neurips-2025-llm-pysc2-starcraft-ii-lear.tldr: LLM-PySC2 exposes the full StarCraft II action space to language models and reveals persistent decision-making and multi-agent coordination difficulties.

paragraphs: PHANTOM evaluates whether models can detect hallucinated answers in financial question answering over long documents. This setting combines several demands: precise numbers, specialized financial language, and evidence that may be difficult to locate within a large context. The benchmark is designed to capture these demands together in hallucination-detection evaluation.

Construction begins with a seed collection linking a question, an answer, and a document chunk. Answers may be correct or hallucinated, and human annotators validate the examples. The collection is then expanded to vary context length and the placement of relevant information. Those variations let the benchmark examine detection when the surrounding material and evidence location change.

The reported evaluations show that out-of-the-box models face severe difficulties detecting real-world hallucinations in long contexts. Fine-tuning open-source language models on PHANTOM provides promising directions for improvement. The contribution is therefore both a comparison resource and evidence that financial hallucination detection requires attention to document structure, context length, and domain-specific accuracy.
neurips-2025-phantom-a-benchmark-for-hal.tldr: PHANTOM benchmarks hallucination detection in long financial documents and finds substantial challenges for out-of-the-box models.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting must decide where to place more primitives and where fewer will suffice. The paper argues that allocating them mainly through rendering loss can favor low-frequency regions, leaving fine texture insufficiently modeled. CDC-GS introduces a separate signal based on visual complexity to guide that allocation.

The method measures complexity using high-frequency wavelet components from the training images. Gaussians contributing to visually complex image regions are treated as representing complex scene regions. It estimates each primitive's local density using the inverse geometric mean of distances to neighboring primitives. Comparing complexity with density then guides which primitives should be densified or pruned.

The intended relationship is that more complex regions receive a higher concentration of primitives. Experiments report substantially better rendering quality than baselines using the same number of Gaussians, making spatial allocation central to the improvement. The accompanying analysis indicates that this complexity-based signal provides guidance complementary to rendering loss, helping direct representational capacity toward fine detail that loss alone can underemphasize.
neurips-2025-reframing-gaussian-splattin.tldr: CDC-GS allocates Gaussian primitives according to visual complexity and local density, improving rendering quality at the same primitive count.

paragraphs: A learned vehicle-routing solver may work well at the capacity limit used during training yet struggle when that limit changes. This paper investigates that problem through the capacity-constrained vehicle routing problem. Its empirical analysis finds that existing neural optimization methods overfit constraint values, performing satisfactorily within only a narrow range of capacity settings.

The proposed response has two components. A training scheme explicitly includes different degrees of constraint tightness, and a multi-expert module learns a more broadly adaptable solving strategy. Together, these changes make variation in the constraints part of what the model learns, rather than treating one fixed constraint value as representative of the whole problem.

Experiments cover both capacity-constrained routing and its version with time windows. Across varying levels of constraint tightness, the method reports superior performance and effective mitigation of the observed overfitting. The findings highlight constraint variation as an important dimension of generalization: success on routing instances at one setting does not establish adaptability across differently constrained versions of the task.
neurips-2025-rethinking-neural-combinato.tldr: Training across constraint tightness levels with a multi-expert module improves neural routing solvers' adaptability to changing capacity and time-window constraints.

paragraphs: SkyLadder examines whether language models should use long context windows throughout pretraining. In a controlled study with a fixed token budget, the authors find that shorter-context models consistently outperform their longer-context counterparts. This motivates changing the context window over training to balance standard performance, long-context ability, and computational efficiency.

The proposed method transitions from shorter windows to longer ones. Earlier training therefore uses a smaller context, while later training introduces longer sequences. The aim is to preserve the benefits observed with short-context pretraining while still developing the ability to handle long inputs. The paper reports that this schedule preserves strong standard benchmark performance and matches or exceeds baseline long-context results.

Experiments train 1B-parameter models with contexts reaching 32K and 3B-parameter models with 8K contexts, using 100B training tokens. Reported improvements reach 3.7% on common benchmarks, alongside training speed gains of up to 22% over baselines. These findings support context-window scheduling as a practical choice affecting both model quality and training efficiency.
neurips-2025-skyladder-better-and-faster.tldr: SkyLadder moves from short to long context windows during pretraining, improving benchmark performance and training speed in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Programmatic weak supervision combines noisy labeling functions to produce labels without manually annotating every data point. A label model must reconcile these imperfect sources. This paper investigates an approach that represents plausible labelings as a polytope, a geometric region of possibilities, and chooses a labeling within that region.

The authors propose Bayesian Balsubramani-Freund, or BBF, to study this strategy theoretically. BBF implicitly constructs the region of plausible labelings and selects an interior solution. The analysis establishes several statistical properties, including posterior log-concavity, the form of the solution, consistency, and convergence rates. These results provide a mathematical account of a strategy motivated by earlier empirical success.

The experimental study compares BBF with twelve baseline label models on eleven datasets. Against other Bayesian models and models that do not use data-point features, BBF matches or exceeds performance on eight datasets. The contribution combines statistical foundations with competitive empirical results, with the reported comparison specifically identifying the categories of label models for which BBF performs favorably.
neurips-2025-statistical-analysis-of-an-.tldr: BBF gives a Bayesian formulation and statistical guarantees for combining noisy labels through an interior solution among plausible labelings.

paragraphs: Language-model training becomes harder to schedule when workloads continue growing beyond a predetermined compute budget. Warmup-stable-decay schedules offer flexibility but require explicit decay phases to assess progress. Weight averaging offers another route, with additional memory costs. This paper revisits schedule-free optimization as an approach suited to continuously scaling training.

The authors analyze SF-AdamW theoretically and empirically, describing how it moves through a river-like structure in the loss landscape. They show that its dynamics implicitly perform weight averaging without the memory overhead of an auxiliary averaging procedure. This helps explain why the method can work effectively without dedicated learning-rate decay phases.

The analysis also motivates a refined schedule-free variant that is more robust to momentum and performs better with large batch sizes. These changes address limitations of the original method in those settings. Together, the explanation and refinement support schedule-free optimization as a practical approach to language-model training whose duration or scale need not be fixed in advance.
neurips-2025-through-the-river-understan.tldr: The paper explains schedule-free optimization through implicit weight averaging and improves its robustness to momentum and large batches.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether transformers can learn reasoning patterns that remain useful when a problem requires longer chains than those encountered during training. It studies synthetic state-tracking tasks with gradient-descent training, allowing the authors to prove how length generalization can emerge in specific mathematical settings.

For tasks with simpler algebraic structure, such as cyclic-group composition, training on short chains of constant length produces a solution pattern that extends to much longer chains. More complex tasks, including symmetric-group composition, use a recursive self-training curriculum. This curriculum progressively builds longer reasoning and generalizes beyond the training horizon, up to the natural limit of the studied setting.

The authors also provide an optimization-based guarantee that constant-depth transformers can learn the studied state-tracking problems in NC1. This exceeds the prior TC0 barrier if the conjectured distinction between those complexity classes holds. The contribution is a proof of learnability through training, with different mechanisms for simpler and more complex tasks, rather than an unrestricted claim about length generalization in arbitrary reasoning problems.
neurips-2025-transformers-provably-learn.tldr: The paper proves length-generalizable transformer reasoning on synthetic state-tracking tasks, using short-chain training or recursive self-training depending on task structure.

paragraphs: Robot task planning must turn language and visual information into sequences that respect implicit constraints. Language and vision-language models provide useful prior knowledge, but can struggle with long plans and symbolic grounding. UniDomain addresses the narrow or handcrafted planning domains often used to connect these models with symbolic planners.

The framework extracts atomic planning domains from 12,393 manipulation videos and combines them into a unified PDDL domain. This resource contains 3,137 operators, 2,875 predicates, and 16,481 causal edges. For a target class of tasks, UniDomain retrieves relevant atomic domains and systematically merges them into a task-relevant meta-domain for zero-shot planning.

The approach makes demonstrated manipulation knowledge reusable when constructing domains for unseen tasks. Experiments on diverse real-world tasks show zero-shot solutions to complex tasks, with reported gains of up to 58% in task success and 160% in plan optimality over state-of-the-art LLM and LLM-PDDL baselines. These results support learning and recombining symbolic planning knowledge from demonstrations as a route to broader robotic task planning.
neurips-2025-unidomain-pretraining-a-uni.tldr: UniDomain learns a reusable symbolic planning domain from manipulation videos and recombines relevant parts to plan complex unseen robot tasks.

paragraphs: WolBanking77 provides a research dataset for recognizing banking-related intentions expressed in Wolof. The motivation is a gap in intent-classification research, which has concentrated on languages with abundant data. Spoken interfaces are particularly relevant where a language is widely used orally and many potential users do not rely on written communication.

The dataset contains 9,791 banking-domain text sentences and more than four hours of spoken sentences. By including text and speech, it supports investigation of both language understanding and speech recognition. The paper also examines the dataset's contents in depth, giving researchers a basis for understanding the material used in its evaluations.

The authors evaluate multiple text and voice models and report baseline F1 scores for language-processing models and word error rates for speech-recognition models. They describe the results on the current dataset as promising and provide comparisons between models. The main contribution is a shared Wolof resource, accompanied by baseline measurements and released code, that enables further research on banking intent recognition in a low-resource language.
neurips-2025-wolbanking77-wolof-banking-.tldr: WolBanking77 introduces Wolof banking text and speech data with baseline evaluations for intent classification and speech recognition.
